query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles to maintain structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service regimes is governed by the formation and stability of a self-limiting, passivating oxide shell (e.g., Cr2O3 or similar) on their surface. This oxide shell, formed from one or more of the alloy’s oxyphilic elements (such as Cr or Al), suppresses atomic diffusion and phase segregation at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic (high-entropy) nanoparticles with a homogeneous solid-solution structure that include one or more oxyphilic elements capable of forming stable oxides.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the nanoparticle composition by preparing two sets: one containing the oxyphilic element(s) (e.g., with Cr) and one in which that element is significantly reduced or omitted, while keeping other processing conditions identical.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature environments typical for catalytic operation (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric application (473–1923 K) in an oxidizing atmosphere that promotes the formation and retention of the passivating oxide layer.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, stable passivating oxide shell on the nanoparticle surface.
generation.mechanism: At the high operational temperatures, the oxyphilic component(s) in the alloy preferentially oxidize to form a self-healing, compact oxide coating. This layer acts as a diffusion barrier, inhibiting surface segregation and coarsening, and thereby preserving the nanoparticle's solid-solution structure and catalytic/thermoelectric functionality. In contrast, nanoparticles lacking this oxide-forming element will have fewer barriers to high-temperature elemental migration and phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles containing the oxide-forming element (e.g., Cr) will show significantly improved structural and chemical stability under high-temperature oxidizing conditions by retaining a stable passivating oxide layer and resisting coarsening or phase segregation, relative to the composition without the oxide-forming element which will exhibit signs of instability such as elemental segregation, coalescence, or formation of secondary phases.
generation.baseline: The behavior of multi-element nanoparticles under high temperature in an oxidizing environment when no compositional modification is introduced (i.e., with a balanced, equiatomic mixture including the oxyphilic element).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily in oxidizing or mildly oxidative environments typical of high-temperature catalytic and some thermoelectric applications. Its predictive power may be limited in reducing environments where the formation or stability of the passivating oxide layer is compromised.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of configurational entropy in stabilizing the solid-solution phase is recognized, the extent to which the passivating oxide layer (versus other potential factors such as grain boundary diffusion barriers) dominates stability is not fully quantified. Additionally, the influence of the precise oxide composition and thickness on long-term stability remains to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic nanoparticles via an identical physical or chemical route: one set with a standard composition including an oxyphilic element (e.g., Cr) and the other with that element largely removed (or replaced by a less oxyphilic element). Expose both sets to controlled oxidizing atmospheres at temperatures within the catalytic regime (773–1173 K) for an identical time period. Characterize the nanoparticles pre- and post-exposure using transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS) to assess the presence and integrity of any oxide layer and to detect any signs of elemental segregation or phase change.
measurements: Thickness and composition of the surface oxide layer (using XPS or EDS)
Morphological changes and particle coarsening (using TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of nanoparticles (with and without the oxyphilic element) show equivalent high-temperature structural and chemical stability and no significant difference in oxide layer formation, then the hypothesis that a self-passivating oxide layer governs stability under the specified conditions would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
